summary.text: Bird migration is the seasonal movement of some birds between breeding and wintering grounds, twice a year and usually between northern and southern regions.
Food seems to be the main motive, and the long days of the northern summer give breeding birds extra time to feed their young.
Timing seems to be controlled mainly by day length, and migrating birds find their way using the Sun, stars, the Earth's magnetic field and mental maps.

facts.label: Record holder
facts.value: Arctic tern, between Arctic breeding grounds and the Antarctic

facts.label: Long-distance migrants
facts.value: About 1,800 of the world's 10,000 bird species

facts.label: Arrow stork
facts.value: A stork found in 1822 carried an African-wood arrow

facts.label: Common pattern
facts.value: North in spring to breed, south in autumn

facts.label: Partial migration
facts.value: Only some populations of a species migrate

items.prompt: A householder keeps hummingbird feeders full all winter, and some birds that would normally leave stay. What does that suggest about the cause of migration?

options.label: Cold weather alone is the main driver
Finding enough to eat appears to be the main motivation
Predators in the north force birds out
Nest sites run out in winter

items.explain: The primary motivation for migration appears to be food; some hummingbirds choose not to migrate if fed through the winter.

items.prompt: Populations that nest farthest north winter farthest south, jumping over populations that nest nearer the south. What is this called?

options.label: Chain migration
Partial migration
Nomadism
Leap-frog migration

items.explain: In leap-frog migration, birds that nest at higher latitudes spend the winter at lower latitudes, bypassing sedentary populations.

items.prompt: A falcon on Mediterranean islands waits until autumn to raise its chicks. What is the likely reason?

options.label: Its chicks are fed on small birds passing south on migration then
Summer heat on the islands is too fierce for chicks
Autumn is when the islands' own birds nest
It waits for the Mediterranean sea to cool

items.explain: Eleonora's falcon breeds very late, coordinated with the autumn passage of southbound passerine migrants, which it feeds to its young.

items.prompt: Birds heading south spread out at first, then many squeeze into a few corridors along mountains and coasts. What might help them?

options.label: Such corridors can offer updrafts and winds and avoid wide open water
Narrow corridors keep different species apart so they cannot compete
Every bird follows one fixed route out and back each year
Birds prefer land because they cannot steer by stars over water

items.explain: Flyways often follow mountain ranges or coastlines and may take advantage of updrafts and wind patterns or avoid geographical barriers such as large stretches of open water.

items.prompt: A bird that flies north to breed lays more eggs than a close relative living year-round in the tropics. What advantage helps?

options.label: Northern nests face no predators at all
Tropical days are too short to raise young
Long northern summer days give parents extra time to feed the young
The warm northern summer makes eggs hatch faster

items.explain: The longer days of the northern summer give breeding birds extended time to feed their young, helping diurnal birds produce larger clutches than related non-migratory species in the tropics.

items.prompt: In 1822 a white stork was found in Germany with an arrow made of central African hardwood. What did that suggest?

options.label: Storks had been carried north by people on long boat trips
Storks can travel from central Africa to Europe on long migrations
Storks spend their winters under water, like swallows
Storks stay in one area all year round, wherever they hatch

items.explain: The Pfeilstorch provided some of the earliest evidence of long-distance stork migration.
